name: Guyliner / kohl

lead: Guyliner is eyeliner worn by men, and kohl, a soft dark powder, is among the oldest eye cosmetics, worn by Egyptian men and women of all classes. The payoff is stronger contrast around the eye, so the gaze looks darker, more intense and more defined.

The term became popular in the early 2000s emo scene. In appearance forums men's liner is discussed for a more intense or hunter-eyed look. No research was found on how liner changes perceived attractiveness in men.

paras: Dark pigment is placed along the lash line, which increases contrast and can make the eye look larger or more defined. Traditional kohl was made from stibnite or galena, while Western products generally use carbon or charcoal.

Studies since the early 1990s have found high lead levels in some kohl products, and lead exposure has been linked to anemia and developmental effects, though some research disputes the links. The FDA does not list kohl as an approved color additive and considers it unsafe, with import and sale in the US illegal. Western commercial eyeliners generally use other pigments.

angle.text: Men use eyeliner or kohl to make the eyes look darker and more intense, a visible change as soon as it is applied. The pigment raises contrast around the eye for a more defined gaze. The style runs from ancient Egyptian use to 2000s emo guyliner.

lead: Guyliner is eyeliner worn by men, and kohl is the soft, usually black eye cosmetic it descends from. Both are used to define the eyes: Wikipedia describes liner as able to make eyes look wider or smaller, create winged or cat-eye shapes, and, when applied along the waterline (tight lining), make lashes appear to start farther back so they look longer [1]. In appearance forums men's eyeliner is discussed as a way to give the eyes a darker, more intense look.

Traditional kohl was made by grinding stibnite (antimony sulfide), while many modern and homemade versions use galena (lead sulfide), and Western manufacturers generally use carbon or charcoal [2]. Egyptians of all social classes are reported to have worn it from about 3100 BCE, with men and women both appearing in tomb depictions [1][2].

The term guyliner became popular in the early 2000s emo scene, partly through bands such as Fall Out Boy and Panic! at the Disco [1]. No studies were found on guyliner's effect on perceived attractiveness, while research on lead in some traditional kohl is described below.

paras: Wikipedia describes liquid, powder pencil, wax pencil, kohl, gel, cake, shimmer and felt-tip liners, each giving a different effect, from sharp winged lines with liquid to smudged soft looks with kohl [1]. Winged and cat-eye styles extend the line outward, and tight lining places pigment right against the lash roots; waterproof formulas are preferred for that technique because of its proximity to the eye's surface [1].

Dark eye lines were used in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia; possible reasons include shielding skin from sun and warding off the evil eye [1]. Kohl was worn in Egypt from about 3100 BCE, reportedly protecting against eye ailments and glare, and the Arabic word kuhl gave rise to both kohl and alcohol [2]. Pharaoh Hatshepsut's kohl included charred frankincense, the first recorded use of that resin [2]. Lead isotope analysis suggests Nubians also used kohl in the Middle Bronze Age [2].

Use spread across North Africa, the Middle East, the Horn of Africa, West Africa and India, where kajal is made from soot and is central to classical dances such as Bharatanatyam [2]. In West Africa kohl is described as worn by both sexes at weddings and festivals [2]. In the 1960s liquid liner produced thick black and white lines associated with Mary Quant, and heavy liner later became associated with goth, punk and emo styles [1]. Guyliner entered popular usage in the 2000s [1].

In the early 1990s studies found lead levels up to 84 percent in some commercial kohl samples, and a study about a decade later found lead in about a third of Egyptian and Indian samples [2]. Lead-contaminated kohl has been linked to higher blood lead levels, with possible effects including anemia, developmental delay, lower IQ, seizures and in severe cases death, though other studies dispute these links [2]. A 2016 Pakistani study reported elevated lead in some women's nail samples and estimated that about 5.2 percent of the lead in surma was bioavailable [2].

The US FDA does not list kohl among approved color additives and considers it unsafe, partly because of lead exposure risk [2]. Wikipedia also reports a 2010 French study in which certain lead compounds from ancient Egyptian kohl raised nitric oxide production at very low concentrations, and a test in which kohl inhibited some bacteria in the lab [2].
No studies found on guyliner and appearance. Published research on kohl concerns lead content, blood lead levels and laboratory antimicrobial tests [2].
